title: Office UPS: batteries, inverter and transformer
summary: Office UPS units hold one to four 12 V sealed lead-acid batteries, an inverter that makes mains AC, a charger, a heavy transformer and a fan. Turn it off and unplug the battery before opening: it makes mains voltage from its battery even with the cord pulled.

steps.text: Unplug the UPS from the wall and every device from it. Press and hold the power button until it switches off and goes silent.
steps.warn: A UPS makes 120 V or 230 V AC from its battery even when unplugged. Treat its outlets and insides as live until the battery is out.

steps.text: Open the battery door: on most units a front panel slides or pops off, or a plate on the underside unscrews.
Pull the battery out by its tab and unplug its connector or the spade terminals. Do this before opening anything else.
steps.warn: Keep tools away from the battery terminals. A short across them can melt a spanner.

steps.text: Measure each battery after it has rested a few hours. 12.6 V or more is full, about 12.2 V is half, below 11.8 V is flat. Below 10.5 V it has been flat a long time and may only partly recover. Swollen or cracked cases: recycle. See test_lead_acid.
Open the case: undo the screws on the underside, back and sides and slide the cover off.
Wait 5 minutes, then measure DC volts across the large capacitors on the board. Discharge any that show more than about 30 V with a resistor tool (see safety_discharge_capacitor) and measure again.
steps.warn: Board capacitors can hold mains-level voltage for minutes after the unit is off.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring. Unplug the leads between the board, the transformer and the battery connector.
Unbolt the transformer: 2–4 bolts through its base. It weighs about 2–8 kg depending on the unit.
Take the main board out whole if you might reuse it as an inverter. Otherwise take the fan, relays, fuse holder, outlets, the mains inlet and the cord.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Batteries.** 12 V sealed lead-acid, most often 7–9 Ah, one to four per unit (two in series makes 24 V). Even tired ones run LED lights, radios and alarms. Many recover some capacity after a long slow charge.
- **The whole UPS.** The best use is often intact: a ready-made battery charger and inverter. Keep a working unit for a router, a radio, a CPAP or a laptop.
- **Transformer.** Heavy iron transformer with a low-voltage winding; a good start for a battery charger or rewinding project.
- **Main board.** Power MOSFETs on heatsinks, relays, a 12 V fan, fuses.
- **IEC outlets and inlet, cord.**

## Running a UPS from bigger batteries

You can wire a bigger battery bank of the same voltage in place of the small batteries, with a fuse close to the battery and thick enough cable (see skill_dc_wiring and reference_wire_gauge). Know the limits:

- Small UPS units are built for 5–15 minutes of running. Long runs at high load overheat them. Keep the load well under half the rating on the label.
- The built-in charger is small (often under 1–2 A), so it can take days to refill a large bank. Charge big banks separately.
- Many small units make a stepped "modified sine" output. Fine for chargers, lights and laptops; motors and some medical devices may run hot or noisy.
- Some units won't start without mains present, and many draw several to tens of watts just being on.

## Variations

- Rack-mount and large floor-standing UPS units hold strings of batteries at 48 V up to several hundred volts DC. Those are lethal and need training to dismantle; see ups_large.
- Some newer small units use lithium iron phosphate batteries instead of lead-acid.

## What to leave

- Batteries with swollen, cracked or leaking cases.
- The plastic case.
